benchmarks.note: different service (the hose, not the valve), six example vehicles from $162 (2013 Tundra) to $268 (2008 Audi A6); labor $145.99 on every one, parts $15.83-$122.35. Shown only to place a small crankcase-ventilation job at a mobile mechanic

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build. Where the PCV valve is sold as a separate part it is a cheap part and a short job, and the price is almost all labor. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Corolla about $67-$168; midsize 2017 Accord 2.4L about $100-$221; truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $78-$189; luxury 2015 Lexus ES 350 about $67-$168. A supportable range for a separate valve is therefore about $65-$220, which sits close to the benchmarks ($76-$220 across RepairPal $124-$173, AutoNation Mobile Service $80-$220 and FIXD $76-$92). Parts are solid: each class has a genuine list price from a dealer catalog page for the example vehicle and year ($8.46 Corolla, $61.27 Accord 2.4L, $28.55 F-150 5.0L, $8.46 ES 350). The lows for economy and midsize are new aftermarket valves on pages naming the vehicle and year ($7.26 and $39.63). For the truck the only aftermarket valve verified costs more than the genuine one at list, and for the luxury car no aftermarket valve was verified, so those two lows are the lowest verified discounted price of the genuine valve ($17.62 and $6.57); on the Corolla the discounted genuine valve ($5.89-$6.06) is also cheaper than the aftermarket one. How solid the labor times are: weak, which is why confidence is low. No maker-stated time for replacing only the valve, printed with a unit, was found for any class, so all four classes use the same two general do-it-yourself statements, 30 minutes (a parts retailer's guide) and 30 to 60 minutes (a parts marketplace's guide by a named author); neither is a flat-rate book time and neither is for the example vehicle. The cross-checks agree the job is short where the valve is easy to reach: Subaru prints 0.2 (no unit) for 'PCV VALVE R&R' on the 2017-2018 Impreza, Nissan's Sentra bulletin implies 0.1 hr (0.5 hrs with the valve against 0.4 hrs without), FCA allows 0.3-0.5 Hrs. on the Grand Wagoneer including a ventilation test, Hyundai allows 1.0 M/H on the Sonata 2.5T including cleaning the intake, and a parts seller's install times for truck valves run from 10 minutes to 1 hour. Warranty times this short mean many shops will simply bill their minimum charge, usually half an hour to an hour. Two limits: no stated time was found for an engine where the valve sits under or behind the intake manifold, which is the long version of this job (RepairPal's 'an hour or two' and AutoNation Mobile Service's '1 to 2 hours' are the only signs of it and are other estimators' figures, so they are not used); a hard-to-reach valve can cost more than the built totals. Engines with the valve built into the valve cover or an oil separator (the Accord V6 valve is noted 'Part included with valve cover'; on Volkswagen's turbo four the unit is quoted at $78-$140) are outside this unit. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis. Review note (2026-11-20): both ends of every labor range rest on one general do-it-yourself guide (30 to 60 minutes); the retailer guide first used for the low end could not be confirmed on re-read and is now a cross-check only.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis, a new grommet or PCV hose (Subaru says to replace the hose with the valve as a set on the 2017-2018 Impreza), thread sealer where the valve screws into the engine, shop supplies and sales tax. Where the valve sits under the intake manifold, expect intake gaskets and more labor. Where it is built into the valve cover or an oil separator, the whole cover or separator is replaced instead, which is a different and dearer job. A valve that has failed can leave oil in the intake or air filter, and cleaning that is extra.
